title: Why Your Growing Business Still Feels Like It's All on You
guestBio: Amanda Carlson is the founder of Muse Multimedia, a brand strategy and web design studio helping entrepreneurs close the gap between their business's visible presence and its underlying clarity. With a background in theater marketing, Amanda brings a storytelling lens to brand messaging, systems, and the founder friction that grows quietly inside successful businesses. She works with women leaders to untangle what their business is trying to tell them before adding another layer of complexity.
excerpt: Your business is growing — so why does it still feel like everything lands on you? Amanda Carlson of Muse Multimedia joins Aimee to unpack the founder friction hiding inside success. This conversation will change the way you listen to what your business is asking for.
metaDescription: Amanda Carlson of Muse Multimedia helps growing founders spot the real friction behind delegation struggles, identity pressure, and messaging gaps.
keyTakeaways: Founder friction is the invisible weight that accumulates when your business has outgrown the way it is still being supported, and growth alone does not make it disappear.
A new website, another system, or more content can look like the answer when the real issue is a lack of clarity underneath the visible problem.
Before using AI or any amplification tool, you must first clarify your message — because AI magnifies what is already there, including the confusion.
Perfectionism and busywork are often a form of delay, a way of avoiding a decision that feels too uncertain or too exposing to make.
Separating your identity from your business is not a luxury — it is the strategic move that allows you to evolve your role as the business grows.
Learning from a decision requires pausing long enough to actually absorb it, rather than sprinting straight to the next problem on the list.
The three starting questions are: What decision are you delaying? What work follows you home? And what part of the business only functions because someone keeps rescuing it?

pullQuotes.text: Clarify before you amplify. AI will take whatever you give it and make it louder — including the confusion.
The business becoming your identity is not a badge of honor. It is a warning sign.
Friction is not failure. Friction is information.
You do not need another giant to-do list to begin listening to what your business is telling you.

quiz.title: What Kind of Friction Is Running Your Business Right Now?
quiz.description: This isn't a quiz about what you're doing wrong — it's a mirror. Answer honestly and discover which pattern of founder friction is most alive in your business right now, and what it's trying to tell you.

A.name: The Clarity Seeker
A.description: You are in a season of genuine reinvention, and the friction you feel is the gap between where your business is and where your vision is pulling you. You have outgrown your old messaging, your old methods, or both — and some part of you knows it, even when it's hard to name. Your instinct is to rebuild from the inside out rather than slap a new coat of paint on something that needs a new foundation. This episode will give you the language and the permission to stop adding more and start getting clear first.

B.name: The Reluctant Delegator
B.description: You believe in your team — in theory. But in practice, you find yourself re-doing work, jumping in before anyone asks, and quietly keeping the whole thing afloat through sheer personal effort. You are not a control freak; you are someone who cares deeply and hasn't yet found a system that makes letting go feel safe. This episode will challenge you to look honestly at the roles, expectations, and processes behind the delegation struggles — and consider that the fix might start with clarity, not trust.

C.name: The Identity Untangler
C.description: The business is succeeding, but somewhere along the way it became hard to know where the company ends and you begin. You make decisions emotionally because the stakes feel personal — because they are. Your brand, your offers, your role are all woven into your sense of self in ways that make it hard to evolve any of them without it feeling like a loss. This episode will invite you to create just enough distance to see your business clearly again — not to care less, but to lead better.

D.name: The Perfectionist in Pause
D.description: You know what needs to change. You might have known for a while. But something keeps you in refinement mode — tweaking, researching, preparing — rather than deciding. It feels responsible, but it's costing you more than you realize in energy, momentum, and the compounding weight of an unmade choice. This episode will name that pattern with warmth and zero judgment, and offer you a different way to move forward that doesn't require everything to be perfect before you begin.

questions.question: When you think about the part of your business that feels heaviest right now, your first instinct is to:

options.text: Audit what's not working and figure out the real root cause before doing anything else.
Find someone to take it off your plate — if only you could trust it would actually get done right.
Wonder whether the whole thing needs a rethink, because it doesn't feel like you anymore.
Add it to the list and keep moving, because stopping to examine it feels like a luxury.

questions.question: When you consider rebranding or updating your messaging, you feel:

options.text: Ready — the current messaging no longer reflects what you actually do or who you serve.
Cautious — you want it to be clear enough that your team can use it without always coming back to you.
Vulnerable — it requires you to be honest about how you and the business have changed.
Overwhelmed — you've been meaning to address it, but there's always something more urgent.

questions.question: When a decision keeps getting delayed in your business, it's usually because:

options.text: You don't have enough clarity on the direction yet, and you refuse to decide without it.
You need to make sure the right person is in place to execute it before you commit.
The decision requires you to let go of something that has been central to your identity.
You keep finding one more thing to research, refine, or finalize before you're ready.

questions.question: If someone asked what your business is really trying to tell you right now, you would say:

options.text: That it needs a clearer foundation — not more features or content built on top of confusion.
That it needs better systems and people who can hold things without you catching every ball.
That it needs me to decide who I want to be in it — because I've changed and the business hasn't caught up.
Honestly? I've been too busy to hear it. But that question makes me want to stop and listen.

questions.question: When you imagine stepping back from the day-to-day operations of your business, you feel:

options.text: Excited but uncertain — you know it's necessary, but the clarity underneath isn't there yet.
Nervous — not because you don't want to, but because you're not sure anyone else can hold it.
Conflicted — because you're not sure who you are when you're not in the middle of it.
Far away from that reality — there are too many active fires to even think about it.

questions.question: When you finish a big project or decision, you typically:

options.text: Pause to evaluate what worked, what didn't, and what it tells you about where to go next.
Hand it off and start thinking about how to make sure the next one runs without you.
Feel a mix of relief and grief — like something ended that was also part of who you were.
Move immediately to the next thing on the list, because slowing down feels dangerous.

content:
You built something real. The revenue is there. The clients are coming. By every external measure, this is working — and yet, somehow, everything still lands on you. Every decision, every workaround, every loose end that threatens to unravel the whole thing. If that sounds familiar, this episode was made for you.

In Episode 84 of The Manage Her® Podcast, Aimee Rickabus sits down with Amanda Carlson, founder of Muse Multimedia, for a conversation that goes far beneath the surface of brand strategy. This is about what happens inside a growing business when the structure holding it up is still built for a version of you — and a version of your company — that no longer exists.

The Problem With Adding More

Amanda came to brand strategy through theater marketing, and that storytelling lens shapes everything about how she sees a business. When founders come to her, they often arrive with a clear request: a new website, a better content strategy, a rebrand. And she has learned to pause before delivering exactly what they asked for.

Because what shows up on the surface — the outdated messaging, the website that no longer converts, the brand that feels off — is rarely the actual problem. It is a symptom. The root is almost always a clarity issue. The business has evolved, but the foundation underneath it has not kept pace. Pouring more resources, more tools, or more content on top of that gap does not close it. It buries it deeper.

This is what Amanda calls founder friction — the accumulated weight of a business that has grown past the way it is still being operated. It is quiet. It does not show up in your revenue numbers. But it shows up in how you feel at the end of every week.

Success Can Still Feel Heavy

One of the most important things Aimee and Amanda name together in this episode is the particular loneliness of struggling inside a successful business. When things look fine from the outside, it is hard to justify the weight you are carrying on the inside. You might tell yourself you have no right to feel this stretched. That you should be grateful. That the friction you feel is just the cost of building something meaningful.

But Amanda reframes that narrative entirely. Friction is not failure. Friction is information. Your business is trying to tell you something — and the heaviness you feel is not a character flaw. It is a signal worth listening to.

The challenge is that most founders are not trained to listen that way. They are trained to fix, to add, to optimize. So when the friction shows up, the instinct is to reach for another solution rather than ask what the problem actually is.

Clarify Before You Amplify

Amanda introduces one of the sharpest ideas in this episode when the conversation turns to AI. She is not anti-technology — far from it. But she offers a warning that every founder using AI tools needs to hear: AI will amplify whatever you give it, including the confusion.

If your messaging is unclear, AI-generated content will produce more of that unclarity, faster and at higher volume. If your brand voice is undefined, AI will fill the gap with something generic that sounds like everyone else. The tool is only as useful as the clarity you bring to it. And that clarity — the kind that knows exactly who you are serving, what you actually offer, and why it matters — is not something you can outsource or automate. It has to come from you first.

This is not just a content strategy point. It is a leadership point. The work of getting clear on your message is the same work as getting clear on your role, your direction, and the kind of company you are actually trying to build.

When the Business Becomes Your Identity

Perhaps the most personal stretch of this conversation arrives when Amanda and Aimee begin talking about what happens when the line between founder and business disappears entirely. It can feel like dedication. It can look like passion. But when the business is your identity, your ability to make clear-eyed decisions about it becomes severely limited.

You cannot objectively evaluate something you have fused yourself to. You cannot evolve a role you cannot separate yourself from. And you cannot let go of tasks, systems, or ways of operating if releasing them feels like releasing a piece of who you are.

The invitation Amanda extends is not to care less — it is to create just enough separation to see clearly. To be able to look at your business the way a trusted advisor would, with love and honesty in equal measure, and ask: what is actually working here, and what is working because I keep personally rescuing it?

Perfectionism, Busywork, and the Decision You Keep Delaying

Perfectionism gets named in this episode for what it often really is: a delay tactic. When you are not ready to make a decision — or when a decision feels too uncertain, too exposing, or too final — it is remarkably easy to stay busy instead. Refining the thing. Perfecting the draft. Researching the options one more time. It feels productive. But it is a way of avoiding the moment when you actually have to choose.

Amanda does not shame this. She normalizes it — and then gently points to the cost. Every delayed decision is a piece of friction that stays in your body, follows you home, and shows up in the quality of your leadership. The antidote is not just making decisions faster. It is creating enough stillness to actually learn from the decisions you make, rather than immediately sprinting to the next problem.

Three Questions to Start Listening

Amanda closes the conversation with a starting point that requires no new tool, no new system, and no consultant. Just honest attention. She asks you to notice three things: the decision you keep delaying, the work that follows you home at the end of the day, and the part of your business that only functions because someone — usually you — keeps rescuing it.

Those three answers are not a to-do list. They are a map. They show you where the friction lives, and they point you toward the clarity that has to come before anything else can change.

If your business is growing and it still feels like everything is on you, you are not doing it wrong. You are simply at the edge of the next evolution — and this conversation will help you take the first honest look at what that actually requires.
